I simply cannot conceive of what else the Court would like EPA to say.
II
[In part II of his dissent Justice Scalia argues that the majority fails 
to give appropriate Chevron deference to the EPA’s conclusion that “air 
pollutant” in the Clean Air Act was meant to refer to contaminants in the 
air near the surface of the Earth in the United States, not to substances 
that collect in the upper atmosphere and are distributed relatively 
uniformly around the globe. He then concluded:]
The Court’s alarm over global warming may or may not be justified, 
but it ought not distort the outcome of this litigation. This is a 
straightforward administrative law case, in which Congress has passed a 
malleable statute giving broad discretion, not to us but to an executive 
agency. No matter how important the underlying policy issues at stake, 
this Court has no business substituting its own desired outcome for the 
reasoned judgment of the responsible agency.

1. Resources, Records and Review of Inaction. Justice Stevens’s opinion 
in Massachusetts v. EPA notes that “some debate remains * * * as to the rigor 
with which we review an agency’s denial of a petition for rulemaking.” This 
statement somewhat obscures the true state of affairs, for the Supreme Court 
had never before decided whether such denials were reviewable at ah. The 
Court then goes onto rely on authority from the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, 
particularly American Horse Protection Ass'n v. Lyng, 812 F.2d 1 (D.C. Cir. 
1987). Indeed, Justice Stevens’s analysis closely tracks the opinion by Judge 
Wilhams in Lyng when pointing out that refusals to initiate rulemaking “are 
less frequent, more apt to involve legal as opposed to factual analysis, and 
subject to special formahties, including a public explanation.” (citing 5 U.S.C. 
§ 555(e)). The court then goes on to say that such review is “extremely limited” 
and “highly deferential,” without explaining why this should be the case.

promulgate a particular rule is a decision that, while not occurring with the
